strengths: Provides a clear conceptual connection between practical bidirectional IMF implementations (DSBM/ASBM) and the IPF procedure, introducing the IPMF viewpoint as a possible unifying perspective.
Includes a theoretical convergence analysis for the 1D Gaussian case with quantitative exponential rates, plus a lemma characterizing Gaussian plans as entropic OT plans.
Empirically evaluates the proposed perspective across several settings: high-dimensional Gaussians, 2D toy data, an SB benchmark, colored MNIST, and CelebA.
The paper is generally well-organized and includes experimental details/hyperparameters in the appendix, supporting reproducibility of the empirical part.
weaknesses: The main observation is largely definitional: reinterpreting the practical bidirectional IMF procedure as combining Markovian and IPF projections is straightforward from the existing update equations. No new algorithm is actually proposed; the method is essentially existing DSBM/ASBM with a new name.

The theoretical convergence result is restricted to 1D Gaussians with one intermediate time point, while the abstract and introduction claim convergence under more general settings and a unified framework. General convergence remains a conjecture, so the central claims are not adequately supported.

Experiments primarily vary the starting process of existing DSBM/ASBM rather than comparing IPMF against pure IMF, pure IPF, or other state-of-the-art SB solvers. There is little direct evidence that the IPMF viewpoint improves performance or robustness compared to prior methods.

On the SB benchmark, the reported metrics are often substantially worse than the best benchmark algorithms, especially for high-dimensional cases and ε=10. The paper does not sufficiently analyze or explain these failures, which undermines claims about convergence quality.

The paper does not provide a controlled ablation isolating the effect of the combined IPF+IMF projections versus the standard bidirectional IMF heuristic, making the practical significance of the IPMF formulation unclear.

There are notation and presentation issues (e.g., inconsistent projection indices in the definition of q^{4k+3}, dense theoretical derivations with possible gaps) that reduce clarity and make the theoretical contribution harder to verify.

The claimed potential impact on diffusion distillation and rectified flows is speculative and not empirically demonstrated; the paper does not show that IPMF actually mitigates error accumulation in such settings.

strengths: Identifies an interesting conceptual connection: the commonly used bidirectional implementation of IMF can be rewritten as alternating Markovian/reciprocal projections with IPF-like marginal projections, which the authors call IPMF.
Provides a theoretical convergence analysis for the 1D Gaussian case, including quantitative contraction bounds and a discussion of the interaction between IPF and IMF projections.

Includes a broad set of experiments—multivariate Gaussians, 2D toy data, the Schrödinger Bridge benchmark, colored MNIST, and CelebA—to empirically study different starting processes and algorithm variants.
The paper is generally well-structured and the problem setting is relevant to the Schrödinger Bridge and diffusion/flow matching communities.
weaknesses: The central novelty is limited: the paper mostly reinterprets/renames an existing practical heuristic (bidirectional IMF used in DSBM/ASBM) as IPMF. It does not introduce a new algorithmic mechanism that materially changes training or inference; the experiments largely run existing DSBM/ASBM algorithms with different initial couplings.

The main theoretical result is restricted to 1D Gaussians (and mostly N=1 or continuous-time IMF), while the paper repeatedly claims a path toward a unified framework and convergence under general settings. No general convergence proof or even a multivariate Gaussian proof is provided; the conjecture remains unsupported.

The experimental evaluation does not convincingly demonstrate that IPMF is competitive with state-of-the-art Schrödinger Bridge methods. On the SB benchmark, several DSBM/ASBM variants are far worse than the best benchmark algorithm (e.g., DSBM-IMF at D=128, ε=10 has cBW2-UVP ≈ 362 versus best ≈ 1.31), yet the text downplays these failures.

The paper lacks appropriate baselines and ablations for a new method. Because IPMF is not a new algorithm, the experiments mainly compare different starting processes of DSBM/ASBM; there is no comparison against IPF and IMF as standalone methods under controlled settings, and no clear evidence that IPMF improves over existing practice.

Several mathematical and notational issues reduce clarity and technical confidence: e.g., q^{4k+3} is written as proj_R(q^{4k+1}) when it should involve q^{4k+2}; the introduction contains a contradictory statement about IMF decreasing forward KL and increasing reverse KL; index notation in the discrete projection is inconsistent.

The claimed asymptotic convergence factors α and β in Theorem 3.2 are not clearly shown to be <1 for all stated settings, and their dependence on arbitrary initial parameters is not made explicit or interpretable. The proof is deferred to an appendix and relies heavily on known Gaussian formulas.

The image-translation experiments are mostly qualitative or use FID/CMMD curves without strong quantitative comparisons to other unpaired translation methods. No statistical significance or robust evaluation protocol is provided.

The reproducibility statement is weak: no code release or computational resources are specified, and the empirical claims would be difficult to reproduce exactly. The broader impact statement is trivial.

The paper overclaims significance, e.g., suggesting IPMF opens a unified framework and may improve rectified flows/Stable Diffusion 3, but provides no experimental or theoretical evidence for these downstream claims.

strengths: The paper identifies a novel connection between the practical bidirectional IMF heuristic and IPF, formalizing IPMF as a unified procedure that alternates IMF and IPF projections. This gives theoretical grounding to common practice in DSBM/ASBM.

Provides a rigorous convergence proof for the 1D Gaussian case with explicit exponential rates, including lemmas on Gaussian plans as entropic OT plans and contraction properties. The analysis is non-trivial and well-supported in the appendix.

Extensive experiments across multivariate Gaussians, 2D toy data, SB benchmark, colored MNIST, and CelebA, considering multiple starting processes (IMF, IPF, independent) to demonstrate convergence. The study supports the claimed generality.
The paper is generally clear, with reproducibility details, hyperparameters, and code references. The significance of a unified perspective on SB algorithms is potentially impactful.
weaknesses: The theoretical convergence result is limited to 1D Gaussians (and N=1 for discrete time), while the main claim of convergence under more general settings remains a conjecture. No general convergence theorem is provided, which weakens the central theoretical contribution.

The proposed IPMF procedure is not a new practical algorithm: it is a reformulation of existing bidirectional IMF implementations (DSBM/ASBM). The experiments do not show performance improvement, only that various initializations converge, and in some cases (ε=0.1) IPF/independent starts yield noticeably worse metrics.

The paper contains an inconsistency/typo in the introduction about KL directions: it states IMF decreases forward KL and may increase reverse KL, whereas IMF is designed to decrease reverse KL. This should be corrected to avoid confusion.

The empirical evaluation lacks statistical significance tests or error bars; some benchmark results are taken from prior work, making it unclear which results are newly generated. Ablations on iteration counts, computational cost, or comparison to one-directional IMF failure are limited.
The claims about opening a 'unified framework' and overcoming error accumulation in rectified flows are speculative and not directly validated. The practical impact is therefore currently modest.

strengths: Provides a useful unified perspective that connects the heuristic bidirectional IMF procedure to IPF via the proposed IPMF framework, clarifying how existing SB algorithms alternate between Markovian and proportional projections.
Derives exponential convergence bounds for IPMF in the Gaussian setting under several configurations, with detailed proofs in the appendix.
Includes a broad set of experiments across Gaussian examples, 2D illustration, the Schrödinger Bridge benchmark, and image translation tasks.
The reformulation has potential relevance for understanding error accumulation in SB/rectified-flow-style methods.
weaknesses: The core theoretical observation that bidirectional IMF can be rewritten as alternating IPF and IMF projections is largely algebraic and may not constitute a sufficiently significant conceptual advance for a top-tier venue.

The convergence guarantee is restricted to Gaussian distributions and, for D>1, to D-IMF with N=1 and ε≫0; the general convergence claim remains a conjecture, so the paper overclaims 'convergence under various settings' and a 'unified framework' relative to the established theory.

The experiments do not demonstrate a new competitive algorithm: they mainly run existing ASBM/DSBM implementations from different starting processes. On the SB benchmark, results are often far from state-of-the-art, e.g., DSBM-IMF at D=128, ε=10 reports 362% cBW2-UVP, undermining claims of reliable convergence.
The paper's practical significance for foundation models/rectified flows is speculative and not directly validated.
Empirical comparisons lack error bars/statistical significance and fair apples-to-apples protocol details in several places, making it hard to judge robustness.
Formatting and clarity issues are substantial: repeated 'Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Size' text, broken equations, corrupted references, and messy figure/table presentation degrade readability.
No code release or reproducibility artifact is referenced, despite extensive experimental claims.

strengths: The paper offers a conceptually clean re-derivation: it shows that the heuristic bidirectional modification of IMF (used in DSBM/ASBM and related methods) is exactly the alternation of IMF projections and IPF projections, thereby giving the previously ad-hoc procedure a principled name (IPMF) and a unifying interpretation. This is a useful clarification for the community.

The theoretical analysis for the Gaussian case is thorough. Theorem 3.1 (characterizing optimality via the matrix Ξ(P,Σ,Σ̃)) and Theorem 3.2 (exponential convergence of parameters, KL divergence, means, covariances, and optimality matrix) are non-trivial, and the appendices contain detailed derivations (Lemmas B.1–B.10, B.5/B.6 for the multidimensional and 1D cases).

The empirical study is reasonably broad: high-dimensional Gaussians (D=128), 2D toy visualization, the SB benchmark with the cBWW2-UVP metric, and real image data (colored MNIST and CelebA), spanning both continuous-time DSBM and discrete-time ASBM implementations.
The paper is generally well organized, the procedure diagrams (Fig. 1) are intuitive, and the code/data sources for DSBM, ASBM and SDE-Edit are referenced, which supports reproducibility.

The demonstration that IPMF can be initialized from arbitrary couplings (e.g., Ind p0 → p0, Inverted 7, SDE-Edit couplings) and still converge is a concrete, empirically-supported insight that goes beyond simply restating existing algorithms.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the central claim. The main 'new' result is that the heuristic bidirectional IMF already used in Shi et al. (2023) and Gushchin et al. (2024) equals the composition of IMF and IPF steps. This is a re-interpretation/re-naming of existing algorithms rather than a new algorithm or a new capability that improves on prior SB solvers.

Theoretical contribution is restricted to Gaussians. Theorem 3.2 and all supporting lemmas assume Gaussian marginals and Gaussian starting couplings, with additional conditions on ε, D, and the initial optimality matrix. The claimed general convergence ('General conjecture') is explicitly unproven and is only validated empirically; no partial results (e.g., local convergence, contraction in general settings, or explicit counterexamples where it fails) are provided.

No clear practical improvement. The experiments do not show that IPMF outperforms the existing bidirectional IMF implementations it abstracts; Table 1 shows DSBM-IMF/ASBM-IMF are often similar to or worse than the 'best algorithm on benchmark' row and competitive alternatives, and the FID/MSE plots show different starting processes only trade off fit-to-target versus feature preservation. Thus the framework's practical value beyond interpretability is unclear.

Weak/incomplete baseline comparison. Since the practical algorithm is unchanged from DSBM/ASBM, the paper should either (a) compare against a genuinely different method (e.g., IPF/Sinkhorn-based diffusion SB solvers, SF2M) more thoroughly, or (b) demonstrate a setting where starting from an arbitrary coupling actually helps. Neither is convincingly shown.

The claim of a 'unified framework for solving SB problems' is overstated given the evidence. A genuine unification would require either broader theory (beyond Gaussians) or a demonstration that IPMF can solve problems (e.g., multimodal or real data distributions) where IPF or one-directional IMF fail. The current experiments largely confirm that the existing heuristic works, which was already known.

The paper does not clearly identify the failure modes of IPMF or contrast with cases where standard IMF/IPF are preferable, so the reader does not gain actionable guidance for choosing among the methods.

Presentation issues: the running header 'Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Size' appears throughout (likely a template artifact), and the main text does not always distinguish clearly between claims proven for Gaussians and claims conjectured in general; this could mislead readers about the strength of the theoretical results.

strengths: Formalizes the heuristic bidirectional IMF as Iterative Proportional Markovian Fitting (IPMF), revealing a clear and useful connection between IPF and IMF: the heuristic effectively alternates between IPF and Markovian/reciprocal projections.

Provides a rigorous Gaussian convergence analysis with explicit exponential rates, including an interesting optimality-matrix characterization of Gaussian entropic OT plans and a detailed treatment of IPF/IMF updates.

Empirically validates convergence across several settings: high-dimensional Gaussians, 2D toy data, the Schrödinger Bridge benchmark, and real image translation tasks, including non-standard initial couplings.
The paper is generally well written, with helpful diagrams (IPF/IMF/IPMF overview) and extensive appendices covering continuous-time formulations and experimental details.
The proposed perspective has plausible practical value, e.g., for understanding error accumulation in bidirectional IMF/DSBM/ASBM and potentially for rectified-flow-style methods.
weaknesses: The main theoretical convergence result is limited to Gaussian distributions and to restricted settings: for D=1 with any epsilon but only IMF/D-IMF; for D>1 only D-IMF with N=1 and large epsilon. The general convergence claim remains a conjecture, so the central unifying claim is not fully proven.

Algorithmic novelty is modest: IPMF is essentially the existing bidirectional DSBM/ASBM heuristic with arbitrary initial couplings. The paper does not propose a new practical algorithm or demonstrate consistent improvement over prior methods.

The empirical evaluation is not fully convincing for practical impact. Image-translation results are mostly qualitative or plotted diagnostics (FID/MSE), without strong quantitative comparisons; on the SB benchmark, IPMF variants are often not better than baseline methods and can be much worse in some settings.

Claims about unifying SB methods and overcoming error accumulation in one-directional IMF/rectified flows are not fully supported by the experiments or theory; the large-epsilon condition in the D>1 theorem may not cover practical low-epsilon regimes.

There are minor notational/presentational issues, e.g., inconsistent projection indices (e.g., q^{4k+3} vs proj_R(q^{4k+2})) and Theorem/Lemma numbering in the appendices, which can make the analysis harder to follow.
